messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: random effects model in Stan
parts:
Hi,

Can somebody advice on the size of nonlinear mixed effects model that could be solved in Stan in reasonable time? For example items that are manufactured in batches exhibit intra-batch variability (items within same batch are different) while average for each batch is also different. This could be handled by two level hierarchical model and thus the number of parameters to estimate grow with increasing  # of batches. I wonder how many batches one may reasonably consider and are there any tricks to overcome dimensionality explosion problem. For instance, nonlinear mixed effects model might involve solution of ODEs.

Thank you,
Linas

This I don't know.

Krzysztof
 

Thank you,
Linas

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: random effects model in Stan
parts:
Stan is so impressive when it comes to many random effects, but the real bummer are ODEs! Just read the autodiff paper on arXiv on the scaling of the ODE system size and you quickly see how expensive ODEs are. On a different note, I just recently simplified an ODE Stan model from using ODEs to using an approximation to the ODE. I had 1400 subjects in the data set and the run time went down from 3 days to only ~4h (!) a factor of more than ~15x speedup (the model was still non-linear, just not using ODEs).

Long story short: Think twice if you can avoid the ODE... although we are working on improving these things, but for structural reasons, the price to pay for ODEs will be high regardless.

Sebastian

parts:
On Friday, May 6, 2016 at 4:57:40 PM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
Krzysztof,

Impressive. Is your model nonlinear?

Bayesian chest-thumping? :P  The model is a Weibull-uniform mixture (to inflate the tail, so that's the three parameters) with truncation (so the data
are {delay, max_delay}.
What do you mean by dropping batches? Simply ignoring data for those batches?

Yeah, or running the model in windows.  At some point extra batches just don't provide any more info 
on hyper-parameters.  Run the model on two windows and compare estimates of the parameters
you care about.  If they're not stable over time (batches) you'd like to know that anyway.  I guess you
could summarize prior batches as priors into a new run but if you have enough data to be taxing
Stan that probably doesn't get you much extra in terms of estimates.
 
 

Thank you,
Linas
